e-6313.knowledge_point: Reducing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve to a Definite Integral
e-6313.problem: Find a definite integral with respect to $\theta$ that is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int \limits_{C} (y^2-x) \, \textrm ds,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r = \cos{\theta}\:$ for $0 \le \theta \le\dfrac{ \pi}4.$
e-6313.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}  f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\cos^2\theta$ and $y=\cos\theta \sin{\theta}$, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}4.$

Now, if $f(x,y) =y^2-x$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \text{ }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta ({sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1) \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta (-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({y}^{2}-x)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{4}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

e-6314.knowledge_point: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Given in Polar Form
e-6314.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{y^2}$ along the polar curve $r=1$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\leq \theta \leq \dfrac\pi 2.$
e-6314.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}  f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\cos\theta$ and $y=\sin\theta$, where $\dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}2.$

Now, since $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2+y^2}{y^2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}{csc}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-(0-\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

e-6315.knowledge_point: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Using Substitution
e-6315.problem: Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle\int_\limits{C} xy(1-x^2) \,\textrm{d}s$, where $C$ is the polar curve $r=\cos{\theta}\:$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
e-6315.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}  f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) \,\sqrt{r^2 + \left(\dfrac{\textrm d r}{\textrm d \theta}\right)^2}\,\textrm d \theta\,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\cos^2\theta$ and $y=\cos\theta\sin\theta$, where $0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y) = xy(1-x^2)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-({cos}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}) \\  & ={cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )=-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy(1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\cos\theta,$ $\textrm d u=-\sin\theta\,\textrm d \theta$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta (1-{cos}^{4}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  & ={\int }_{1}^{0}-{u}^{3}(1-{u}^{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{3}-{u}^{7})\,\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{{u}^{4}}{4}-\frac{{u}^{8}}{8}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{8})-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2+y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π?

a
2∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
b
4∫0πcos2⁡θdθ
c
8∫0πcos⁡θdθ
d
2∫0πsin⁡θdθ
e
8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Since x²+y²=r²=4sin²θ and ds=√(r²+(dr/dθ)²)dθ=√(4sin²θ+4cos²θ)dθ=2dθ, the integral equals 8∫₀^π sin²θ dθ, which is option e.

\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2+y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π?

a
2∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
b
4∫0πcos2⁡θdθ
c
8∫0πcos⁡θdθ
d
2∫0πsin⁡θdθ
e
8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=2sin2⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ and y=2sin2⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2+y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2sin⁡θcos⁡θ)2+(2sin2⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+4sin4⁡θ=4sin2⁡θ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=4sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2sin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2sin⁡θ)2+(2cos⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ=4(sin2⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫C(x2+y2)ds=∫0πf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π4sin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ.

content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

∫C(x2+y2)ds=∫0πf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π4sin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ.

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx2yds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for −π4≤θ≤π4?

a
2∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
b
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
c
2∫−π/4π/4sin2⁡θcos⁡θdθ
d
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
e
22∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Here x=√2 cosθ, y=√2 sinθ, and ds=√2 dθ because r is constant. Thus x²y ds=4sinθ cos²θ dθ, giving option b directly. Options a, d, and e also equal the same value, zero, since their integrands are odd over symmetric limits.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx2yds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for −π4≤θ≤π4?

a
2∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
b
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
c
2∫−π/4π/4sin2⁡θcos⁡θdθ
d
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
e
22∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2y, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2cos⁡θ)2⋅2sin⁡θ=22sin⁡θcos2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2)2+02=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cx2yds=∫−π/4π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4π/422sin⁡θcos2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms b: x²y=2√2 sinθ cos²θ and ds=√2 dθ, so their product gives 4sinθ cos²θ dθ. This agrees with the earlier answer. Although a, d, and e also evaluate to zero by odd symmetry, b is the direct polar-coordinate conversion.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve to a Definite Integral
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cy4x2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=cot⁡θ for −π4≤θ≤−π8?

a
∫−π/4−π/8cos⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
b
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
c
∫−π/4−π/8sin⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
d
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
e
∫−π/4−π/8cos2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: In polar coordinates, y⁴/x²=r²sin⁴θ/cos²θ=sin²θ. Since r′=−csc²θ, ds=√(cot²θ+csc⁴θ)dθ=√(sin²θ cos²θ+1)/sin²θ dθ. Multiplication cancels sin²θ, giving option b.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}?$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )=-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cy4x2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=cot⁡θ for −π4≤θ≤−π8?

a
∫−π/4−π/8cos⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
b
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
c
∫−π/4−π/8sin⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
d
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
e
∫−π/4−π/8cos2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ and y=cos⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤−π8.

Now, if f(x,y)=y4x2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos4⁡θ(cos2⁡θsin⁡θ)2=sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(cot⁡θ)=−1sin2⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(cot⁡θ)2+(−1sin2⁡θ)2=cos2⁡θsin2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θ.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cy4x2ds=∫−π/4−π/8f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θ⋅sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θdθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve to a Definite Integral
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}?$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )=-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ and y=cos⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤−π8.

Now, if f(x,y)=y4x2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos4⁡θ(cos2⁡θsin⁡θ)2=sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(cot⁡θ)=−1sin2⁡θ,

and therefore

Finally, we can write the integral as

before.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2−2y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
∫0π/2sin2⁡θ(1−3sin2⁡θ)dθ
b
∫0π/2sin⁡θ(1−sin⁡θ)dθ
c
 ∫0π/2sin2⁡θ(1−cos2⁡θ)dθ
d
 ∫0π/2sin⁡θ(3−cos6⁡θ)dθ
e
∫0π/22sin3⁡θdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: With r=sinθ, x=sinθ cosθ and y=sin²θ. Thus x²−2y²=sin²θ(cos²θ−2sin²θ)=sin²θ(1−3sin²θ). Also ds=√(sin²θ+cos²θ)dθ=dθ, so option a follows.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-2{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2−2y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
∫0π/2sin2⁡θ(1−3sin2⁡θ)dθ
b
∫0π/2sin⁡θ(1−sin⁡θ)dθ
c
 ∫0π/2sin2⁡θ(1−cos2⁡θ)dθ
d
 ∫0π/2sin⁡θ(3−cos6⁡θ)dθ
e
∫0π/22sin3⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=sin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=sin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=sin2⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=sin⁡θcos⁡θ and y=sin2⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π2.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2−2y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(sin⁡θcos⁡θ)2−2(sin2⁡θ)2=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ−2sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θ(cos2⁡θ−2sin2⁡θ)=sin2⁡θ(1−sin2⁡θ−2sin2⁡θ)=sin2⁡θ(1−3sin2⁡θ).

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(sin⁡θ)=cos⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(sin⁡θ)2+(cos⁡θ)2=1=1.

Finally, we can write the integral as

content.knowledge_point: Reducing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve to a Definite Integral
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}$, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}-2{({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,(1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta (1-3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx4y2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=tan⁡θ for π6≤θ≤π3?

a
∫π/6π/3sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
b
∫π/6π/3sin2⁡θcos4⁡θ+1dθ
c
∫π/6π/3sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ−1dθ
d
∫π/6π/3sin4⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
e
∫π/6π/3sin4⁡θcos4⁡θ−1dθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Since x=r cosθ=sinθ and y=r sinθ=sin²θ/cosθ, x⁴/y²=cos²θ. Also r′=sec²θ, so ds=√(tan²θ+sec⁴θ)dθ=√(sin²θ cos²θ+1)/cos²θ dθ. The cos²θ factors cancel, yielding option a.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}?$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $y=\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$, where $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )=\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx4y2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=tan⁡θ for π6≤θ≤π3?

a
∫π/6π/3sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
b
∫π/6π/3sin2⁡θcos4⁡θ+1dθ
c
∫π/6π/3sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ−1dθ
d
∫π/6π/3sin4⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
e
∫π/6π/3sin4⁡θcos4⁡θ−1dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=tan⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=sin⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=tan⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=sin⁡θ and y=sin2⁡θcos⁡θ, where π6≤θ≤π3.

Now, if f(x,y)=x4y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=sin4⁡θ(sin2⁡θcos⁡θ)2=cos2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(tan⁡θ)=1cos2⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(tan⁡θ)2+(1cos2⁡θ)2=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1cos4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1cos4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1cos2⁡θ.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cx4y2ds=∫π/6π/3f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/6π/3cos2⁡θ⋅sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1cos2⁡θdθ=∫π/6π/3sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ.

content.knowledge_point: Reducing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve to a Definite Integral
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}?$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ and $y=\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$, where $\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )=\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{x}^{4}}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Evaluate the integral ∫C(2y+3x)ds, where the curve C is given in polar form by r=sin⁡2θ for 0≤θ≤π2.

a
2
b
0
c
π−1
d
5
e
3
Submit

decision.explanation: For r=√(sin2θ), r′=cos2θ/r, so √(r²+(r′)²)=1/r on the interior of the interval. Since 2y+3x=r(2sinθ+3cosθ), the integral becomes ∫₀^{π/2}(2sinθ+3cosθ)dθ=[−2cosθ+3sinθ]₀^{π/2}=5.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}(2y+3x)\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }$, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, if $f(x,y)=2y+3x$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }+3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta +\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2x+3y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =(0+3)-(-2+0) \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the integral ∫C(2y+3x)ds, where the curve C is given in polar form by r=sin⁡2θ for 0≤θ≤π2.

a
2
b
0
c
π−1
d
5
e
3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=sin⁡2θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡2θ,y=rsin⁡θ=sin⁡2θ⋅sin⁡θ=sin⁡θsin⁡2θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos⁡θsin⁡2θ and y=sin⁡θsin⁡2θ, where 0≤θ≤π2.

Now, if f(x,y)=2y+3x, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=2sin⁡θsin⁡2θ+3cos⁡θsin⁡2θ=sin⁡2θ(2sin⁡θ+3cos⁡θ).

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(sin⁡2θ)=12sin⁡2θ⋅(cos⁡2θ)⋅2=cos⁡2θsin⁡2θ

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=sin⁡2θ+cos2⁡2θsin⁡2θ=sin2⁡2θ+cos2⁡2θsin⁡2θ=1sin⁡2θ=1sin⁡2θ.

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫C(2x+3y)ds=∫0π/2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/2sin⁡2θ(2sin⁡θ+3cos⁡θ)⋅1sin⁡2θ⋅dθ=∫0π/2(2sin⁡θ+3cos⁡θ)dθ=[−2cos⁡θ+3sin⁡θ]0π/2=(0+3)−(−2+0)=5

content.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s$, where the curve $C$ is given in polar form by $r=2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }$ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }$, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta } \\  & =2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta )\cdot 2 \\  & =-\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +\frac{4{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4{cos}^{2}⁡2\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{4({cos}^{2}⁡2\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡2\theta )}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }\,(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ){|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4([\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}]-[-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}]) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi /2)-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π4.

Now, since f(x,y)=x2−y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2cos⁡θ)2−(2sin⁡θ)2=4cos2⁡θ−4sin2⁡θ=4(cos2⁡θ−sin2⁡θ)=4cos⁡2θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=22+02=4=2.

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫C(x2−y2)ds=∫0π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/44cos⁡2θ⋅2⋅dθ=∫0π/48cos⁡2θdθ=4sin⁡2θ|0π/4=4(sin⁡(π/2)−sin⁡0)=4

content.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ along the polar curve $r=2\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$  

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & =4({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}4\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi /2)-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta | \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ because $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta >0.$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-0-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=sin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=sin⁡θsin⁡θ=sin2⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=sin⁡θcos⁡θ and y=sin2⁡θ, where π4≤θ≤π2.

Now, since f(x,y)=x2+y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(sin⁡θcos⁡θ)2+(sin2⁡θ)2=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=sin2⁡θ=|sin⁡θ|=sin⁡θ.

Notice that |sin⁡θ|=sin⁡θ because π4≤θ≤π2⟹sin⁡θ>0.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(sin⁡θ)=cos⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(sin⁡θ)2+(cos⁡θ)2=1=1.

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

∫Cx2+y2ds=∫π/4π/2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫π/4π/2sin⁡θ⋅1⋅dθ=∫π/4π/2sin⁡θdθ=−cos⁡θ|π/4π/2=−0−(−22)=22

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Given in Polar Form
content.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ along the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+({sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{4}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta | \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ because $\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\,⟹\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta >0.$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-0-(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$ 

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, we now evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot (0-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ along the polar curve $r=3$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(3)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  & =3{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =3({e}^{3}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =3({e}^{3}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Evaluate the integral of the function f(x,y)=xey along the polar curve r=3 for 0≤θ≤π2.

a
9(e−1)
b
9(e2−1)
c
3(eπ/2−1)
d
3(e3−1)
e
3eπ/2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=3cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=3sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=3cos⁡θ and y=3sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π2.

Now, since f(x,y)=xey, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=3cos⁡θe3sin⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(3)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=32+02=3.

We can now write the integral as

∫Cxeyds=∫0π/2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/23cos⁡θe3sin⁡θ⋅3⋅dθ=3∫0π/23cos⁡θe3sin⁡θdθ.

We can solve this using the substitution u=3sin⁡θ, du=3cos⁡θdθ as follows:

3∫0π/23cos⁡θe3sin⁡θdθ=3∫03eudu=3eu|03=3(e3−e0)=3(e3−1)

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Using Substitution
content.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ along the polar curve $r=3$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(3)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{e}^{3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  & =3{\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =3({e}^{3}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =3({e}^{3}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{3}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}({(\frac{1}{2})}^{5/2}-{0}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{5}}} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12

Evaluate the integral of the function f(x,y)=xy3 along the polar curve r=2 for 0≤θ≤π6.

a

b

EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=3cos⁡θ and y=3sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π6.

Now, since f(x,y)=xy3, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ⋅(2sin⁡θ)3=42sin3/2⁡θcos⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=22+02=2.

We can now write the integral as

∫Cxy3ds=∫0π/6f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/642sin3/2⁡θcos⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=82∫0π/6sin3/2⁡θcos⁡θdθ.

We can solve this using the substitution u=sin⁡θ, du=cos⁡θdθ as follows:

82∫0π/6sin3/2⁡θcos⁡θdθ=82∫01/2u3/2du=82⋅25u5/2|01/2=1625((12)5/2−05/2)=1625⋅125=1625⋅142=45

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms 4/5, option a. For r=2, x=2cosθ, y=2sinθ, and ds=2dθ. With u=2sinθ, the integral becomes 2∫₀¹u^(3/2)du=4/5. The solution's sentence giving x=3cosθ and y=3sinθ is a typo; its calculations correctly use r=2.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve Using Substitution
content.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$ along the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{3}} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\sqrt{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}4\sqrt{2}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{sin}^{3/2}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =8\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}({(\frac{1}{2})}^{5/2}-{0}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{5}}} \\  & =\frac{16\sqrt{2}}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{4\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=6$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
after.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(6)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 6\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =6{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =3({(3\sqrt{3})}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 27 \\  & =81\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution u=6sin⁡θ, du=6cos⁡θdθ as follows:

6∫0π/36cos⁡θ⋅6sin⁡θdθ=6∫033udu=6⋅12u2|033=3((33)2−02)=3⋅27=81

content.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the polar curve $r=6$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$
content.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}.$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(6)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}36\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot 6\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ $\text{d}u=6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta $ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot 6\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  & =6{\int }_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3\sqrt{3}} \\  & =3({(3\sqrt{3})}^{2}-{0}^{2}) \\  & =3\cdot 27 \\  & =81\end{aligned}
$$
